I-31.explain: Most recurrent tummy pain in children has no structural cause, so you diagnose functional pain from a typical pattern rather than after exhausting tests.
I-31.hook: Functional = a positive diagnosis, not a dustbin.

checks.q: How should functional abdominal pain in children be diagnosed?
checks.why: Most chronic pain is functional; diagnose it positively from the pattern rather than after endless tests.

I-31.explain: Split causes into functional (IBS, functional abdominal pain) and organic; among organic causes, constipation is by far the commonest one you can fix.

checks.q: Which of these is a functional cause of chronic abdominal pain?
checks.why: IBS is functional; coeliac and choledochal cyst are organic causes.

checks.q: Commonest treatable organic cause of chronic abdominal pain in children?
checks.why: Constipation is the commonest treatable organic cause; coeliac and H. pylori are rarer.

I-31.explain: Functional pain clusters around the umbilicus; pain localised away from it points to a real organ. IBS involves gut-brain sensitivity, not structural damage.
I-31.hook: Far from the belly button = far from functional.

checks.q: Pain located far from the umbilicus suggests what?
checks.why: The further from the umbilicus, the more likely an organic cause.

checks.q: Is IBS associated with structural bowel abnormalities?
checks.why: IBS has no structural abnormality; ulceration suggests IBD, villous atrophy coeliac.

I-31.explain: Night waking is a red flag because functional pain does not wake children. In infants, good growth and development make organic disease unlikely.
I-31.hook: Wakes at night = look for a cause. Growing well = reassuring.

checks.q: Which feature argues against functional abdominal pain?
options: Pain waking the child at night
checks.why: Functional pain never wakes the child at night, so night waking is a red flag.

checks.q: Key question for functional GI complaints in infancy?
options: Is there a family history of IBS?
checks.why: Per the exam key: if somatic development is good, organic causes are unlikely.

I-31.explain: Calprotectin is a neutrophil protein shed in stool when the gut is inflamed, so it separates IBD from functional pain. H. pylori's urease splits labelled urea, detectable in breath.
I-31.hook: Calprotectin = inflammation in a cup; urease = breath test.

checks.q: Best non-invasive test to separate IBD from functional pain?
checks.why: Faecal calprotectin reflects mucosal neutrophil inflammation; CRP is less specific.

checks.q: Which test exploits H. pylori urease activity?
checks.why: H. pylori is urease-positive, so labelled urea is split and detected in breath.

I-31.explain: IBS responds to lifestyle and diet changes (low FODMAP, fibre); the strongest evidence is for CBT because it targets the gut-brain axis. Always treat coexisting constipation.

checks.q: First-line management of IBS in children?
options: Lifestyle change, low FODMAP diet, fibre
checks.why: IBS first line is lifestyle modification, low FODMAP diet and fibre.

checks.q: Best-evidence treatment for functional abdominal pain?
checks.why: CBT has the best evidence; it targets the gut-brain axis.

I-32.explain: Fluid leaves vessels when pushing pressure rises, pulling (oncotic) pressure falls, capillaries leak, or lymph cannot drain it back.
I-32.hook: Push up, pull down, leak, or block.

checks.q: Which is NOT a Starling mechanism of oedema?
checks.why: Oedema comes from LOW oncotic pressure; raised oncotic pressure holds fluid in vessels.

I-32.explain: In a young child with generalised swelling, nephrotic syndrome is commonest; other low-protein or leak states (kwashiorkor, gut, liver, HAE) are the differentials.

checks.q: Commonest cause of generalised oedema in a young child?
checks.why: Nephrotic syndrome is the commonest cause of generalised oedema in young children.

checks.q: Which nutritional disorder causes generalised oedema?
checks.why: Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency) causes oedema; marasmus is wasting without oedema.

I-32.explain: Kwashiorkor lowers albumin, so oncotic pull falls and fluid leaks. Membranous nephropathy shows a thick GBM with granular immune-complex deposits.

checks.q: Mechanism of oedema in kwashiorkor?
checks.why: Low protein intake lowers albumin and plasma oncotic pressure.

checks.q: Membranous nephropathy histology shows which deposits?
checks.why: Membranous: GBM thickening with granular immune complexes; linear IgG is anti-GBM.

I-32.explain: Fluid pools in lax periorbital tissue when lying flat overnight, so swelling shows first around the eyes in the morning. HAE gives recurrent non-itchy swelling without hives.
I-32.hook: Puffy eyes at breakfast; swelling without hives = HAE.

checks.q: Where does nephrotic oedema typically first appear?
checks.why: Lax periorbital tissue collects fluid overnight, so it shows first around the eyes in the morning.

checks.q: Recurrent non-pitting, non-itchy swelling without urticaria suggests?
checks.why: HAE is bradykinin-mediated, so no itch or urticaria, unlike allergic angio-oedema.

I-32.explain: Nephrotic range is heavy proteinuria (UPCR >200) with low albumin. If albumin is low but the urine has no protein, the loss is in the gut or production fails in the liver.
I-32.hook: Low albumin, clean dipstick: look at gut or liver.

checks.q: UPCR threshold for nephrotic-range proteinuria in children?
checks.why: Nephrotic: UPCR >200 mg/mmol with low albumin; 20-200 is sub-nephrotic.

checks.q: Low albumin with negative urine dipstick points to which organs?
checks.why: No proteinuria means the albumin is lost via gut (protein-losing enteropathy) or not made by the liver.

I-32.explain: Treatment depends on which Starling force is wrong. Most childhood nephrotic syndrome (minimal change) responds to steroids; HAE reflects C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency.
I-32.hook: Fix the force; minimal change melts with steroids.

checks.q: Guiding principle for treating oedema?
checks.why: Oedema treatment targets the mechanism, not just the fluid.

checks.q: Hereditary angio-oedema is a deficiency of what?
checks.why: HAE is C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency; bradykinin is raised, not deficient.

I-33.explain: Each 1% dehydration is 10 ml per kg lost, so deficit = % × weight × 10.

checks.q: Fluid deficit in a 10 kg child who is 5% dehydrated?

I-33.explain: Gastroenteritis drives most dehydration; rotavirus causes the most severe diarrhoea in young children. Shigella adds fever, bloody mucus and even seizures.
I-33.hook: Rotavirus = severe watery; Shigella = blood, fever, fits.

checks.q: Commonest cause of severe diarrhoea in young children?
checks.why: Rotavirus is the commonest cause of severe diarrhoea in children.

checks.q: Mucoid-bloody diarrhoea, high fever and seizures suggest which pathogen?
checks.why: Shigella causes dysentery with fever and can trigger seizures; cholera is watery.

I-33.explain: Diarrhoea removes fluid from the extracellular space, so blood becomes concentrated (higher haematocrit and protein). Rotavirus destroys villi, reducing absorption.

checks.q: In diarrhoeal dehydration, what happens to haematocrit?
checks.why: ECF volume falls, so haematocrit and plasma protein concentrate and rise.

checks.q: Rotavirus damages the gut by what mechanism?
checks.why: Rotavirus destroys villi; cAMP-toxin is cholera, invasion is Shigella.

I-33.explain: Water leaves cells in hypernatraemia, giving a doughy skin feel. Children maintain BP by tachycardia and vasoconstriction until very late, so hypotension means imminent arrest.

checks.q: Doughy skin in a dehydrated infant suggests which type?
checks.why: Doughy skin is classic for hypernatraemic dehydration.

checks.q: Hypotension in a shocked child is what kind of sign?
checks.why: Children compensate well; hypotension appears late and signals impending arrest.

I-33.explain: Always check sodium. Brain cells adapt to high sodium by making osmoles, so fast correction drives water into them and causes cerebral oedema.
I-33.hook: High sodium: slow down, max 0.5 per hour.

checks.q: Maximum rate of sodium correction in hypernatraemia?
checks.why: Correct no faster than 0.5 mEq/L/hr to avoid cerebral oedema.

checks.q: Rapid correction of hypernatraemia causes what?
checks.why: Adapted brain cells take up water if sodium falls fast; myelinolysis follows fast hyponatraemia correction.

I-33.explain: Without shock, ORS replaces the deficit over hours. In shock, give a crystalloid bolus. Rotavirus vaccine prevents the commonest severe cause.
I-33.hook: No shock: ORS 50/4h. Shock: 10 ml/kg saline.

checks.q: ORS regimen for dehydration without shock?
checks.why: Give ORS 50 ml/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance.

checks.q: Shock bolus volume in a dehydrated child (0.9% NaCl)?
checks.why: Notes (NICE 2020): 10 ml/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus; older texts/WHO say 20 ml/kg.

I-34.explain: Every fluid plan adds four parts: resuscitation, deficit, maintenance and ongoing losses. Standard maintenance fluid is dextrose in normal saline (D5NS).

checks.q: Standard maintenance fluid in children per the notes?
checks.why: Standard maintenance is D5NS (5% dextrose in 0.9% saline); plain D5W is hypotonic.

I-34.explain: Holliday-Segar scales fluid to energy use: heavier children need less per kg, so 100, then 50, then 20 ml/kg/day.

checks.q: Holliday-Segar daily maintenance for the second 10 kg?
checks.why: 100 ml/kg for first 10 kg, 50 ml/kg next 10 kg, 20 ml/kg above 20 kg.

I-34.explain: Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells (risking lysis and hyponatraemia), so isotonic fluids are used after the neonatal period. Neonates already have excess sodium/water until their postnatal diuresis.
I-34.hook: Neonate: no salt till they pee it off.

checks.q: Beyond the neonatal period, which fluid tonicity is used?
checks.why: Hypotonic fluid risks RBC lysis and hyponatraemia, so isotonic fluid is used.

checks.q: When is sodium added to neonatal IV fluids?
checks.why: Sodium is withheld until the postnatal diuresis starts, around day 2-3.

I-34.explain: Too much fluid backs up into tissues, liver and lungs. Illnesses that raise ADH make children retain free water, so give only 50-80% of maintenance.

checks.q: Which finding suggests fluid overload?
checks.why: Overload causes oedema, hepatomegaly, crackles and weight gain; the others are dehydration.

checks.q: In meningitis with high ADH, restrict maintenance to what?
checks.why: High ADH states (meningitis, pneumonia, post-op, head injury) need 50-80% of maintenance.

I-34.explain: 20 kg: 10×100 + 10×50 = 1500 ml/day, about 60 ml/h by 4/2/1. A 3 kg neonate on day 1 at 60 ml/kg/day needs about 180 ml/day.

checks.q: Daily maintenance fluid for a 20 kg child?
checks.why: 1000 ml (first 10 kg) + 500 ml (next 10 kg) = 1500 ml/day, ≈60 ml/h.

checks.q: Day-1 maintenance for a 3 kg term neonate?
checks.why: 60 ml/kg/day × 3 kg ≈ 180 ml/day (7.5 ml/h).

I-34.explain: Term neonates start low (50-60 ml/kg/day of 10% glucose) and rise by day 5 as diuresis occurs and feeds build. Older children get isotonic saline with glucose.
I-34.hook: Neonate starts at 60 and climbs to 150.

checks.q: Day-1 IV fluid for a term neonate?
checks.why: Start 50-60 ml/kg/day 10% glucose, rising to 120-150 ml/kg/day by day 5.

checks.q: Maintenance fluid for an older child?
checks.why: Isotonic 0.9% NaCl with 5% glucose; hypotonic 0.18% saline risks hyponatraemia.

I-35.explain: Sex has layers (chromosomes, gonads, genitals) that normally match. Ambiguous genitalia is an emergency because salt-wasting CAH can kill within weeks.
I-35.hook: Ambiguous genitals = check the sodium today.

checks.q: Why is ambiguous genitalia in a newborn an emergency?
checks.why: Ambiguous genitalia is an emergency; salt-wasting CAH can cause adrenal crisis.

I-35.explain: 21-hydroxylase block diverts steroid precursors to androgens, virilising 46,XX girls. In complete androgen insensitivity, 46,XY testes make testosterone the body can't respond to.
I-35.hook: CAH virilises girls; CAIS feminises boys.

checks.q: Commonest cause of ambiguous genitalia in a newborn?
checks.why: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CAH) is the commonest cause.

checks.q: 46,XY, female genitalia, testes, no uterus: diagnosis?
checks.why: CAIS: testes make AMH (no uterus) but androgen receptors fail, so genitals are female.

I-35.explain: SRY turns the gonad into a testis; Sertoli cells make AMH to regress Müllerian ducts, Leydig testosterone virilises. Faulty receptors mean testosterone has no effect.
I-35.hook: SRY builds, AMH erases, testosterone masculinises.

checks.q: Which hormone causes regression of the Müllerian ducts?
checks.why: AMH from Sertoli cells regresses Müllerian ducts; testosterone drives Wolffian development.

checks.q: Androgen insensitivity is a defect of what?
checks.why: Androgen insensitivity is an androgen receptor defect; hormone levels are normal or high.

I-35.explain: Lack of aldosterone in salt-wasting CAH lets sodium fall and potassium rise, typically at 1-3 weeks. Pubic hair needs androgen action, so it is absent in AIS but present in Müllerian agenesis.
I-35.hook: CAH crisis at 1-3 weeks: low Na, high K.

checks.q: When does salt-wasting CAH typically present?
checks.why: Salt-wasting crisis typically appears at 1-3 weeks with low Na and high K.

checks.q: Pubic hair in androgen insensitivity versus Müllerian agenesis?
options: Absent in AIS, present in agenesis
checks.why: Pubic hair needs androgen action: absent in AIS, present in Müllerian agenesis.

I-35.explain: Karyotype first. 17-OH-progesterone builds up behind the 21-hydroxylase block. A 'boy' with no palpable gonads may be a virilised 46,XX girl with CAH.
I-35.hook: No testes felt = assume CAH girl.

checks.q: Screening test for CAH?
checks.why: 17-OHP accumulates behind the 21-hydroxylase block and is the screening test.

checks.q: 'Male' infant with non-palpable gonads: assume what until proven otherwise?
checks.why: Non-palpable gonads = CAH (virilised 46,XX) until proven otherwise.

I-35.explain: Sex assignment needs the full multidisciplinary team. In AIS, gonads are removed after puberty to allow natural oestrogenic puberty first. Hypospadias foreskin is kept for repair.
I-35.hook: Keep the foreskin for the surgeon.

checks.q: Who should decide sex assignment in DSD?
checks.why: Involve the MDT before assigning sex.

checks.q: Timing of gonadectomy in complete androgen insensitivity?
checks.why: Bilateral gonadectomy after puberty lets testes-derived oestrogen drive puberty first.

I-36.explain: Puberty normally begins 8-13 in girls and 9-14 in boys; outside these windows it is precocious or delayed.
I-36.hook: Early: 8 girls/9 boys. Late: 13 breasts/14 testes.

checks.q: Premature puberty in girls is defined as signs before which age?
checks.why: Exam key: secondary sex characteristics before 8 years in girls, 9 in boys.

checks.q: Delayed puberty in boys: no testicular enlargement by what age?
checks.why: Delayed puberty: no breasts by 13 in girls, no testicular enlargement by 14 in boys.

I-36.explain: Girls usually have idiopathic central puberty, boys more often have a brain lesion. Constitutional delay is the commonest cause of late puberty.
I-36.hook: Boys go early? Scan the brain.

checks.q: Central precocious puberty in boys is usually due to?
checks.why: Girls are mostly idiopathic; boys often have an organic CNS cause.

checks.q: Delayed puberty with anosmia suggests which syndrome?
checks.why: Kallmann: GnRH deficiency with anosmia due to olfactory/GnRH neuron migration failure.

I-36.explain: In central puberty the pituitary is primed, so GnRH-agonist stimulation raises LH; in peripheral puberty, sex steroids suppress LH/FSH. Oestrogen fuses growth plates in both sexes.
I-36.hook: Central: LH rises. Peripheral: LH flat.

checks.q: In peripheral precocious puberty, LH and FSH are?
checks.why: Peripheral sex steroids feed back and suppress LH/FSH; central shows LH rise on stimulation.

checks.q: Which hormone closes the epiphyseal growth plates?
checks.why: Oestrogen (also from aromatised testosterone) closes growth plates.

I-36.explain: Puberty starts with breast buds in girls and testicular enlargement (≥4 ml) in boys. Virilisation with small testes means androgens come from elsewhere, like the adrenals.

checks.q: First sign of puberty in boys?
checks.why: Testicular enlargement to ≥4 ml is the first sign in boys; thelarche in girls.

checks.q: Early virilisation in a boy with small testes suggests what source?
options: Leydig cell tumour of both testes
checks.why: Small testes with virilisation means androgens are adrenal, e.g. CAH.

I-36.explain: Central puberty may hide a hypothalamic tumour, so image before treating. In primary amenorrhoea, ultrasound shows whether a uterus is present.

checks.q: Required investigation before treating central precocious puberty?
checks.why: MRI brain excludes a CNS lesion before starting GnRH agonist.

checks.q: First imaging in primary amenorrhoea?
checks.why: Pelvic ultrasound shows uterus/ovaries; Müllerian agenesis has normal secondary sex characteristics.

I-36.explain: Continuous GnRH agonist desensitises pituitary receptors and halts central puberty. Benign variants like premature adrenarche or newborn breast buds need only reassurance.

checks.q: Treatment of central precocious puberty?
checks.why: Depot GnRH agonist desensitises the pituitary and stops central puberty.

checks.q: Management of newborn breast enlargement?
checks.why: Neonatal breast enlargement from maternal hormones needs reassurance only.

I-37.explain: SVT is a re-entry circuit through or around the AV node, so it starts and stops suddenly and is the commonest symptomatic tachyarrhythmia in children.
I-37.hook: SVT switches on like a light.

checks.q: Commonest symptomatic tachyarrhythmia in children?
checks.why: SVT is the commonest; it typically starts abruptly.

I-37.explain: WPW has an accessory pathway; long QT syndromes are channel defects, deafness marking the recessive Jervell-Lange-Nielsen. Maternal anti-Ro/La damage the fetal conduction system.
I-37.hook: Jervell = deaf; Ro/La = blocked baby heart.

checks.q: Long QT syndrome with congenital deafness?
checks.why: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen is AR with deafness; Romano-Ward is AD without.

checks.q: Cause of congenital complete heart block?
checks.why: Maternal anti-Ro/La cross the placenta and damage the fetal conduction system.

I-37.explain: Prolonged repolarisation allows early afterdepolarisations, triggering torsades. Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node, breaking re-entry circuits that use it.

checks.q: Long QT syndrome predisposes to which arrhythmia?
checks.why: Prolonged repolarisation triggers torsades de pointes.

checks.q: How does adenosine terminate SVT?
checks.why: Adenosine inhibits the AV node, briefly blocking it and breaking re-entry.

I-37.explain: Infants can't report palpitations; hours of very fast rates exhaust the myocardium and present as heart failure. Syncope without warning suggests arrhythmia rather than a faint.
I-37.hook: Baby SVT = poor feeding, sweaty, failing.

checks.q: Typical presentation of SVT in infants?
checks.why: Infants with rates >220 present with heart failure, not palpitations.

checks.q: Sudden syncope without prodrome suggests what?
checks.why: No warning symptoms points to an arrhythmia; vasovagal has a prodrome.

I-37.explain: In WPW the accessory pathway pre-excites the ventricle, shortening PR and slurring QRS onset (delta wave). Brugada shows coved ST elevation in V1-V3.
I-37.hook: WPW: short PR + delta. Brugada: V1-V3 ST up.

checks.q: Resting ECG finding in WPW?
checks.why: WPW: short PR, wide QRS, delta wave from ventricular pre-excitation.

checks.q: Brugada syndrome ECG pattern?
checks.why: Brugada: pseudo-RBBB with ST elevation V1-V3.

I-37.explain: Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres then fast adenosine; verapamil can cause collapse in infants. Unstable means shock. Long QT gets beta-blockers, complete block a pacemaker.
I-37.hook: Stable: vagal, adenosine. Unstable: shock it.

checks.q: Which drug is contraindicated for SVT in infants?
checks.why: Verapamil can cause cardiovascular collapse in infants; adenosine is first-line drug.

checks.q: Treatment of unstable SVT?
checks.why: Unstable SVT needs synchronised cardioversion.

I-38.explain: Children's BMI changes with age, so obesity is judged on BMI centiles. Most obesity is exogenous (energy excess), not endocrine.
I-38.hook: Plot BMI on a centile chart, not adult cut-offs.

checks.q: How is childhood obesity assessed?
options: BMI centiles for age and sex
checks.why: Children's BMI varies with age, so centiles are used.

I-38.explain: Excess calories accelerate growth, so exogenously obese children are tall with advanced bone age. Endocrine causes slow growth, making them short.
I-38.hook: Tall and fat = food; short and fat = hormones.

checks.q: Height and bone age in exogenous obesity?
checks.why: Overnutrition speeds growth: tall with advanced bone age.

checks.q: Commonest monogenic cause of obesity?
checks.why: MC4R mutations are the commonest monogenic cause of obesity.

I-38.explain: Prader-Willi is a paternal 15q deletion; raised ghrelin drives hunger. Insulin resistance links acanthosis, PCOS and fatty liver.

checks.q: Which hormone is raised in Prader-Willi syndrome?
checks.why: Raised ghrelin drives the hyperphagia in Prader-Willi; GH and IGF-1 are low.

checks.q: Common mechanism of acanthosis nigricans, PCOS and fatty liver?
checks.why: Insulin resistance underlies all three.

I-38.explain: High insulin stimulates skin cell growth, causing velvety dark neck folds. Excess weight stresses the growth plate (SCFE) and narrows the airway (OSA).
I-38.hook: Obese teen limping = SCFE until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Velvety dark skin in neck folds is called?
checks.why: Acanthosis nigricans is the marker of insulin resistance.

checks.q: Obese teenager with knee pain and limp: think of?
checks.why: SCFE often presents with referred knee pain in obese adolescents.

I-38.explain: Very early onset, extreme hunger, delay or dysmorphism suggest a genetic cause. Metabolic syndrome needs at least 3 of 5 criteria.

checks.q: Genetic red flag in obesity: onset before what age?
checks.why: Onset before 5 years is a genetic red flag, with hyperphagia, delay or dysmorphism.

checks.q: Metabolic syndrome requires how many of 5 criteria?
checks.why: Metabolic syndrome: at least 3 of 5 criteria.

I-38.explain: Children copy family habits, so family-based lifestyle change comes first. GLP-1 agonists reduce appetite and are licensed from age 12.
I-38.hook: Whole family changes, not just the child.

checks.q: First-line treatment of childhood obesity?
checks.why: Family-based lifestyle change comes first.

checks.q: From what age is semaglutide licensed for obesity?
checks.why: GLP-1 agonists like semaglutide are licensed for obesity from 12 years.

I-39.explain: Short stature means height more than 2 SD below the mean (about the 2nd centile).

checks.q: Definition of short stature?
checks.why: Short stature is height below -2 SD.

I-39.explain: Most short children are normal variants (familial or constitutional). Hypothyroidism is the most frequent endocrine cause.
I-39.hook: Normal variants first; thyroid tops endocrine.

checks.q: Which is a normal variant of short stature?
checks.why: Familial short stature and constitutional delay are normal variants.

checks.q: Most frequent endocrine cause of growth retardation?
checks.why: Exam key: hypothyroidism is the commonest endocrine cause.

I-39.explain: GH acts via IGF-1 to grow bone; thyroid hormone is also needed. Pathology shows as poor height velocity, crossing centiles downward.

checks.q: Growth hormone mainly acts via which mediator?
checks.why: GH raises IGF-1, which drives bone growth.

checks.q: Which growth pattern suggests pathological short stature?
checks.why: Low height velocity crossing centiles downward signals pathology.

I-39.explain: Familially short children grow normally with bone age matching age. In constitutional delay, bone age lags so they keep growing longer and reach normal final height.
I-39.hook: Familial: bone age = age. Constitutional: bone age behind.

checks.q: Bone age in familial short stature?
checks.why: Familial: bone age equals chronological age; delayed in constitutional delay.

checks.q: Final height in constitutional delay?
checks.why: Delayed bone age means growth continues longer, reaching normal final height.

I-39.explain: Turner can present only with short stature, so every unexplained short girl gets a karyotype. GH secretion is pulsatile, so two stimulation tests are needed.

checks.q: Every unexplained short girl needs which test?
checks.why: Karyotype excludes Turner syndrome, which may present with short stature alone.

checks.q: How many GH stimulation tests confirm GH deficiency?
checks.why: GH deficiency needs two GH stimulation tests.

I-39.explain: Treat the cause: levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, GH for deficiency, Turner and Prader-Willi. Constitutional delay needs only reassurance.
I-39.hook: Thyroid gets thyroxine; constitutional gets reassurance.

checks.q: Treatment of short stature due to hypothyroidism?
checks.why: Treat the cause: levothyroxine.

checks.q: Management of constitutional delay of growth?
checks.why: Constitutional delay ends in normal height, so reassurance.

I-40.explain: Weakness comes from one of four levels: anterior horn cell, nerve, neuromuscular junction or muscle; findings like fasciculations or fatigability localise it.

checks.q: First step in evaluating a weak child?
checks.why: Localise to horn cell, nerve, NMJ or muscle first.

I-40.explain: SMA is SMN1 deletion; Duchenne is X-linked dystrophin absence. Myasthenia attacks postsynaptic ACh receptors; infant botulism comes from honey spores.

checks.q: Genetic cause of spinal muscular atrophy?
checks.why: SMA is due to SMN1 deletion; dystrophin is Duchenne, CTG is myotonic dystrophy.

checks.q: Infant botulism is classically linked to what?
checks.why: Infant botulism comes from ingesting honey spores.

I-40.explain: In myasthenia, repeated use depletes ACh vs blocked receptors, so weakness worsens; Lambert-Eaton improves with use. More SMN2 copies mean milder SMA.

checks.q: How does myasthenic weakness change with repeated use?
checks.why: Myasthenia worsens with use; Lambert-Eaton improves.

checks.q: SMA severity is determined by what?
checks.why: More SMN2 copies produce more protein and milder SMA.

I-40.explain: Fasciculations and areflexia mark lower motor neuron disease (SMA). Gowers sign shows proximal weakness in Duchenne; fatigable ptosis is myasthenia.

checks.q: Floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and areflexia?
checks.why: Tongue fasciculations and areflexia indicate anterior horn cell disease (SMA).

checks.q: Gowers sign is classic for which disorder?
checks.why: Gowers sign reflects proximal weakness in Duchenne.

I-40.explain: GBS shows albuminocytologic dissociation; spirometry tracks respiratory decline. Duchenne muscle breakdown raises CK 10-100x.

checks.q: Typical CSF in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
checks.why: GBS: albuminocytologic dissociation.

checks.q: Serum CK in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
checks.why: Duchenne: CK raised 10-100x.

I-40.explain: GBS: IVIG or plasmapheresis. Infant botulism: human-derived immune globulin. Duchenne: steroids slow decline.

checks.q: Treatment of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
checks.why: IVIG or plasmapheresis; steroids are not effective in GBS.

checks.q: Disease-modifying treatment in Duchenne?
checks.why: Steroids slow decline in Duchenne.

I-41.explain: Platelets and VWF make the first plug at mucosa and skin, so their defects cause mucocutaneous bleeding; clotting factor defects fail deeper, causing joint and muscle bleeds.

checks.q: Joint and muscle bleeds suggest a defect in what?
checks.why: Deep bleeds point to clotting factors; mucocutaneous to platelets/VWF.

I-41.explain: Haemophilia A lacks factor VIII, B factor IX. VWD is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder; ITP antibodies target GPIIb/IIIa.

checks.q: Haemophilia B is deficiency of which factor?
checks.why: Haemophilia A = VIII; haemophilia B = IX.

checks.q: Commonest inherited bleeding disorder?
checks.why: VWD is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder.

I-41.explain: Desmopressin releases stored vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies. ITP IgG is made in the spleen and crosses the placenta.

checks.q: How does desmopressin work in von Willebrand disease?
checks.why: Desmopressin releases vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies.

checks.q: Where are ITP antibodies mainly produced?
checks.why: ITP antibodies are produced in the spleen and can cross the placenta.

I-41.explain: ITP lowers only platelets, giving petechiae and long bleeding time in a well child. Severe haemophilia causes spontaneous haemarthroses.
I-41.hook: Well child + petechiae + low platelets = ITP.

checks.q: Blood count pattern in ITP?
checks.why: ITP gives isolated thrombocytopenia; pancytopenia suggests leukaemia or aplasia.

checks.q: Hallmark of severe haemophilia?
checks.why: Severe haemophilia causes spontaneous joint bleeds.

I-41.explain: Factors VIII and IX sit in the intrinsic pathway, so APTT lengthens and PT stays normal. ITP becomes chronic after a year.

checks.q: Coagulation screen in haemophilia?
checks.why: VIII and IX are intrinsic pathway factors.

checks.q: Chronic ITP is defined as low platelets for how long?
checks.why: Per the notes, chronic ITP = low platelets for more than 1 year.

I-41.explain: Intracranial bleeds in haemophilia can be silent early, so give factor immediately and transfer. Inhibitors need bypassing agents; ITP with only petechiae is observed.
I-41.hook: Head knock in haemophilia = factor now.

checks.q: Haemophilic child with head trauma, no fainting: first action?
options: Immediate factor concentrate, refer to centre
checks.why: Exam key: give factor concentrate immediately and refer to the nearest haemophilia centre.

checks.q: Management of ITP with only petechiae?
checks.why: ITP with only skin signs is observed.

I-42.explain: ADHD is a cross-setting pattern of hyperactivity, impulsivity and/or inattention. Autism combines social-communication deficits with restricted, repetitive behaviours.

checks.q: ADHD symptoms must occur in how many settings?
checks.why: ADHD requires symptoms in ≥2 settings.

checks.q: Which feature defines autism spectrum disorder?
checks.why: ASD: poor social interaction plus repetitive/ritualised behaviours.

I-42.explain: ADHD is highly heritable, with prenatal exposures and prematurity adding risk. Autism is genetic with syndromic links; MMR does not cause it.

checks.q: Approximate heritability of ADHD?
checks.why: ADHD is about 70-80% heritable.

checks.q: Which prenatal drug exposure is linked to autism?
checks.why: Fetal valproate exposure increases autism risk; MMR is not a cause.

I-42.explain: Weak dopamine and noradrenaline signalling in ADHD impairs impulse control, which is why stimulants help. In autism, social cues are not rewarding, so predictable routines calm.

checks.q: Neurotransmitters underactive in ADHD?
checks.why: Weak dopamine and noradrenaline signalling causes impulsivity.

checks.q: Why do routines calm autistic children?
checks.why: Altered connectivity makes social cues unrewarding, so predictable routines comfort.

I-42.explain: ADHD criteria: onset before 12, 2+ settings, 6+ months. Autism shows early with poor eye contact, sameness and stereotypies.

checks.q: ADHD symptoms must start before which age?
checks.why: DSM-5: onset before 12, in ≥2 settings, for ≥6 months.

checks.q: Which is a typical early sign of autism?
checks.why: Poor eye contact, insistence on sameness and stereotypies are typical.

I-42.explain: ADHD is clinical after excluding mimics like hearing loss and absences. M-CHAT screens autism at 18 and 24 months; check hearing before diagnosing and use ADOS.

checks.q: How is ADHD diagnosed?
checks.why: ADHD is clinical; exclude hearing, vision, absences and OSA.

checks.q: Autism screening tool at 18 months and 2 years?
checks.why: M-CHAT-R/F screens; ADOS is the diagnostic observation tool.

checks.q: Before diagnosing autism in a non-verbal child, do which test?
checks.why: Hearing loss can mimic autism, so test hearing first.

I-42.explain: From age 5, methylphenidate is first-line, then atomoxetine or guanfacine. Stimulants raise heart rate and BP and suppress appetite. Autism: early therapy; risperidone for severe irritability.
I-42.hook: Methylphenidate first; watch heart and growth.

checks.q: First-line drug for ADHD from age 5?
checks.why: Methylphenidate is first-line; atomoxetine and guanfacine follow.

checks.q: Which parameter is monitored on stimulants?
checks.why: Monitor heart rate, BP, height and weight on stimulants.

checks.q: Drug for severe irritability in autism?
checks.why: Risperidone treats severe irritability; early developmental therapy is the mainstay.

I-43.explain: pH depends on HCO3:pCO2. SMORE: if pH and pCO2 move the same way it's metabolic; opposite ways, respiratory.

checks.q: pH depends on the ratio of which two values?
checks.why: pH follows the HCO3:pCO2 ratio.

checks.q: pH and pCO2 both low: primary disorder?
checks.why: SMORE: same direction = metabolic; low pH = acidosis.

I-43.explain: A high anion gap means an unmeasured acid has been added; normal gap means HCO3 lost (diarrhoea, RTA). Pyloric stenosis loses HCl.
I-43.hook: High gap = acid in; normal gap = bicarb out.

checks.q: Which causes a high anion gap acidosis?
checks.why: DKA adds ketoacids; diarrhoea and RTA cause normal gap acidosis.

checks.q: Which causes a normal anion gap acidosis?
checks.why: Diarrhoea loses HCO3 with chloride retained, so gap stays normal.

checks.q: Acid-base picture in pyloric stenosis?
checks.why: Vomiting HCl causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

I-43.explain: Lungs compensate within minutes, kidneys over days. In pyloric stenosis, aldosterone saves Na by losing H+, giving paradoxical aciduria.

checks.q: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis?
checks.why: Low HCO3 drives hyperventilation, lowering pCO2.

checks.q: How long does renal compensation take?
checks.why: Respiratory compensation is immediate; renal takes 3-5 days.

checks.q: Paradoxical aciduria in pyloric stenosis is driven by?
checks.why: HCl loss plus aldosterone makes kidneys excrete H+.

I-43.explain: Deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing blows off CO2 in metabolic acidosis. In acute asthma, pCO2 should be low; a normal or rising pCO2 means exhaustion.

checks.q: Deep, rapid breathing in metabolic acidosis is called?
checks.why: Kussmaul breathing blows off CO2.

checks.q: Normal pCO2 in acute severe asthma signals what?
checks.why: A normal or rising pCO2 signals exhaustion and impending failure.

I-43.explain: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3), normally 8-12. Winter's formula predicts pCO2. In metabolic alkalosis, urine chloride separates vomiting from other causes.

checks.q: Normal anion gap range?
checks.why: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3), normal about 8-12.

checks.q: Winter's formula for expected pCO2?
checks.why: Expected pCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2; 0.7 × HCO3 + 20 is for alkalosis.

checks.q: Next step in metabolic alkalosis?
checks.why: Urine chloride separates chloride-responsive causes like vomiting.

I-43.explain: Treat the cause; bicarbonate is not routine. In pyloric stenosis, replace chloride and volume first, operating once Cl and HCO3 normalise because anaesthesia risks apnoea.
I-43.hook: Fix the salts before the knife.

checks.q: Is bicarbonate routine in metabolic acidosis?
checks.why: Treat the cause; bicarbonate is not routine.

checks.q: First priority in pyloric stenosis with alkalosis?
checks.why: Replace chloride and volume first.

checks.q: When to operate on pyloric stenosis?
options: Once Cl and HCO3 are normal
checks.why: Operate after Cl and HCO3 normalise.

I-44.explain: Water follows sodium across cell membranes: low plasma sodium swells brain cells, high plasma sodium shrinks them.
I-44.hook: Low Na swells, high Na shrinks.

checks.q: In hyponatraemia, water moves in which direction?
checks.why: Low plasma sodium makes water enter brain cells.

I-44.explain: Low sodium: SIADH with hypotonic fluids, GI loss, salt-wasting CAH, oedematous states. High sodium: gastroenteritis, poor breastfeeding in week 1, DI.
I-44.hook: Breastfed baby losing weight in week 1 = high Na.

checks.q: Classic iatrogenic cause of hyponatraemia?
checks.why: SIADH combined with hypotonic IV fluids is a classic cause.

checks.q: Hypernatraemia in a week-old breastfed baby suggests?
checks.why: Poor breastfeeding in week 1 causes hypernatraemic dehydration.

I-44.explain: Swelling causes oedema in a rigid skull. Shrinking pulls on bridging veins until they tear.

checks.q: Main brain complication of acute hyponatraemia?
checks.why: Water entering brain cells causes cerebral oedema.

checks.q: Why does hypernatraemia cause intracranial haemorrhage?
checks.why: High Na shrinks brain, tearing bridging veins.

I-44.explain: Hyponatraemia: headache, vomiting, seizures; neonate with low Na and high K suggests CAH. Hypernatraemia: high-pitched cry, doughy skin, seizures.
I-44.hook: Low Na + high K neonate = CAH.

checks.q: Neonate with low sodium and high potassium: diagnosis?
checks.why: Low Na with high K in a neonate suggests salt-wasting CAH.

checks.q: Skin feel typical of hypernatraemia?
checks.why: Hypernatraemia gives doughy skin; shock appears late.

I-44.explain: Paired osmolalities, urine sodium and volume status classify sodium disorders. SIADH: low plasma osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine, euvolaemia, urine Na >30.
I-44.hook: SIADH: dilute blood, concentrated urine, euvolaemic.

checks.q: Which assessment is key to classify hyponatraemia?
checks.why: Plasma/urine osmolality, urine Na and volume status classify it.

checks.q: Urine sodium in SIADH?
checks.why: SIADH: euvolaemic with urine Na >30.

I-44.explain: Seizures from low sodium need 3% saline. SIADH: fluid restriction. Chronic hyponatraemia corrected too fast causes osmotic demyelination; hypernatraemia corrected over 48 hours.
I-44.hook: Low Na: max 8-10/day. High Na: 48 h.

checks.q: Treatment of hyponatraemic seizures?
checks.why: Hyponatraemic seizures need a 3% saline bolus.

checks.q: Too-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes?
checks.why: Raise Na ≤8-10 mmol/L/24 h to avoid osmotic demyelination.

checks.q: Over what period is hypernatraemia corrected?
checks.why: Correct over 48 hours, no faster than 0.5 mmol/L/h.

I-45.explain: Potassium sets the resting membrane potential, so abnormal K disturbs heart and muscle excitability.

checks.q: Main physiological role of potassium?
checks.why: K sets the resting membrane potential; Na drives the upstroke.

I-45.explain: High K: AKI, CAH, DKA, tumour lysis, drugs. In a well infant, a haemolysed sample is commonest. Low K: GI losses, pyloric stenosis, diuretics, insulin, refeeding.
I-45.hook: Well baby with high K? Squeezed heel.

checks.q: Which drug can cause hyperkalaemia?
checks.why: Trimethoprim blocks ENaC like amiloride; furosemide and salbutamol lower K.

checks.q: Commonest cause of high K in a well infant?
checks.why: Haemolysis releases intracellular K, giving a false high.

checks.q: Which can cause hypokalaemia?
checks.why: Insulin drives K into cells; the others raise K.

I-45.explain: High K inactivates fast Na channels, slowing conduction. Salbutamol and insulin activate Na/K-ATPase, shifting K into cells. Low magnesium prevents K correction.

checks.q: How does hyperkalaemia slow cardiac conduction?
checks.why: Partial depolarisation inactivates fast Na channels, slowing conduction.

checks.q: How do salbutamol and insulin lower potassium?
checks.why: They activate Na/K-ATPase, shifting K into cells.

checks.q: Refractory hypokalaemia: which ion to replace?
checks.why: Low K may not correct until magnesium is replaced.

I-45.explain: High K: peaked T, then wide QRS, then sine wave. Low K: weakness, ileus, flat T, U waves.
I-45.hook: Peaked T first; low K gives U waves.

checks.q: Earliest ECG sign of hyperkalaemia?
checks.why: Peaked T waves come first.

checks.q: ECG sign of hypokalaemia?
checks.why: Hypokalaemia flattens T waves and produces U waves.

I-45.explain: Heel-prick samples often haemolyse, so first repeat a free-flowing venous sample. In low K, urine K >20 means renal loss.

checks.q: First step for high K on heel-prick in a well infant?
checks.why: Exclude haemolysis by repeating a free-flowing venous sample.

checks.q: In hypokalaemia, urine K >20 indicates?
checks.why: Urine K >20 means the kidney is wasting potassium.

I-45.explain: With ECG changes, calcium stabilises the myocardium first. Then shift K into cells, then remove it. Low K: oral KCl, IV only diluted, never as a bolus.

checks.q: First drug for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes?
checks.why: Calcium gluconate protects the myocardium first.

checks.q: Which treatment shifts K into cells?
checks.why: Salbutamol shifts K; calcium protects; resin removes.

checks.q: How should IV potassium be given?
checks.why: IV K goes diluted in fluids; a bolus can cause arrest.
